credit: Large-empire outlines adapted (clipped and simplified) from historical-basemaps by A. Ourednik and contributors, GPL-3.0 (this file is therefore offered under GPL-3.0); coastlines and island outlines from Natural Earth (public domain); capital coordinates from Pleiades (CC BY 3.0, pleiades.stoa.org). Schematic zones for small kingdoms and the Herodian tetrarchies were drawn for Scripture Atlas from the sources cited in each period.

precisionLegend.approximate: Adapted from a published dataset or coastline; borders of ancient states were zones, not lines.
precisionLegend.schematic: A coarse zone following natural limits (coast, rivers, wadis, desert edge) named in the sources; not a surveyed border.
precisionLegend.label-only: Location known, extent not known well enough to draw.

periods.name: Patriarchal age
periods.summary: Middle Kingdom Egypt ruled the Nile valley from a new capital, Itjtawy, and pushed its frontier to the Second Cataract. Mesopotamia passed from the Ur III state to rival Amorite dynasties (Isin, Larsa, Mari, Yamhad) until Hammurabi of Babylon unified much of it about 1760 BC. Canaan was a land of small city-states. Genesis sets Abraham's journey from Ur and Harran into Canaan, and Joseph's rise in Egypt, against this background.

powers.name: Middle Kingdom Egypt
powers.note: Nile valley from the Delta to the Second Cataract forts; the dataset polygon is cut at 21.4°N to match the Second Cataract frontier named by Britannica. Itjtawy itself has not been located; the marker is the el-Lisht pyramid field nearby.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc2000.geojson (feature "Egypt"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified; southern cut after Britannica, "Amenemhet I"

powers.name: Mesopotamia (Ur III, then Babylon)
powers.note: The dataset draws the Ur III state (to c. 2004 BC). Afterwards the area was split among Isin, Larsa, Eshnunna and Babylon until Hammurabi (c. 1792–1750 BC) united most of it. The same outline stands for both; borders shifted constantly.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc2000.geojson (feature "Ur"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Amorite kingdoms
powers.note: Rival Amorite states of Syria and Upper Mesopotamia, among them Mari, Yamhad (Aleppo) and Qatna. Shamshi-Adad briefly united the north (c. 1830–1776 BC); Hammurabi destroyed Mari's palace. No single capital.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc2000.geojson (feature "city-states"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Canaanite city-states
powers.note: Many small city-states, no unified kingdom. The outline is the dataset's rough "Canaan".
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc2000.geojson (feature "Canaan"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Mari
powers.note: Amorite kingdom on the middle Euphrates; its palace archive is a key source for the period.
powers.source: Pleiades

powers.name: Yamhad
powers.note: Amorite kingdom centred on Halab (Aleppo).
powers.source: Pleiades

powers.name: Ur
powers.note: Sumerian city named as Abraham's home in Gen 11:31; the identification of "Ur of the Chaldeans" with this site is traditional and widely, but not universally, accepted.
powers.source: Pleiades

powers.name: Harran
powers.note: Upper Mesopotamian city where Terah settled (Gen 11:31-32).
powers.source: Pleiades

powers.name: Elam
powers.note: Kingdom of south-west Iran (Gen 14:1). Shown as a label only: the dataset's "Elam" polygon for 2000 BC lies along the Persian Gulf coast and leaves out Susa, so it was not used.
powers.source: Pleiades (Susa)

periods.debate: Genesis gives no dates that can be tied securely to external history, and scholars disagree on whether, and where, the patriarchal stories fit the second millennium BC. The map shows the political setting usually proposed (c. 2000–1700 BC), not a confirmed date for Abraham.

periods.name: Exodus and settlement
periods.summary: New Kingdom Egypt ruled Canaan through local vassal kings watched from centres such as Gaza, Beth-shean, Sumur and Kumidi. To the north the Hittites, having broken Mitanni, fought Egypt at Kadesh (1275 BC) and later made peace. Around 1200 BC the Hittite empire and many Levantine city-states collapsed; Pharaoh Merneptah's stele (late 13th century BC) is the first mention of "Israel" outside the Bible.

powers.name: New Kingdom Egypt
powers.note: Nile valley outline from the dataset; New Kingdom rule actually reached further south into Nubia (to about the Fourth Cataract), beyond this outline.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1500.geojson (feature "Egypt"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Egypt's Canaanite domain
powers.note: Zone of Egyptian overlordship over Canaanite vassal kings, from the Sinai coast to the edge of Amurru and Kadesh (both lost to the Hittites). Its eastern edge follows the desert margin; its northern edge is only approximate.
powers.source: schematic, after Mandell (TheTorah.com) and De Magistris 2023; coast from Natural Earth

powers.name: Hittite Empire
powers.note: Anatolian empire with its capital at Hattusa; Carchemish governed its Syrian holdings. The polygon comes from a dataset file whose content is not period-specific (see debate); the part overlapping Egypt's zone has been removed.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1500.geojson (feature "Hittites"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified; area overlapping Egypt's schematic zone removed

powers.name: Mitanni
powers.note: Hurrian kingdom that dominated northern Mesopotamia c. 1600–1350 BC. Its capital Washukanni has not been securely located; Tell Fakhariyah (ancient Sikani in Pleiades) is the leading candidate.
powers.source: Met Heilbrunn Timeline; Pleiades (Sikani/Tell Fakhariyah)

powers.name: Assyria
powers.note: Middle Assyrian kingdom, which ended Mitanni's power in the 14th–13th centuries BC.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1500.geojson (feature "Assyria"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.note: Babylonia under the Kassite dynasty (c. 1570–1155 BC).
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1500.geojson (feature "Babylonia"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

periods.debate: The date of the Exodus is disputed: a 15th-century date (from 1 Kgs 6:1) and a 13th-century date (Ramesside setting, Exod 1:11) both have defenders, and many historians doubt that a single migration of the size described can be traced at all. Settlement models (conquest, peaceful infiltration, internal emergence) are also debated. The historical-basemaps file used here (world_bc1500) is largely identical to its 1000 BC and 700 BC files and contains anachronisms, so its shapes are treated as rough.

periods.name: United monarchy
periods.summary: The Bible presents Saul, David and Solomon ruling a single kingdom of Israel from Jerusalem, with neighbouring peoples as subjects or tributaries. Archaeologists agree that a polity existed in the Judean hills; they disagree sharply about its size, wealth and date. The map shows a modest core most scholars can accept, and separately the larger realm as the Bible describes it.

powers.name: Israel: core
powers.note: Core (widely accepted): the Judean hills and the Benjamin plateau around Jerusalem, between the Shephelah and the Dead Sea/Jordan rift. Even this is contested by some minimalists; others would add the central hill country further north.
powers.source: schematic, after Thomas 2016 and Schiffman (COJS); limits follow the Dead Sea, Jordan valley and Shephelah edge

powers.name: Realm per 1 Kgs 4:21 (debated)
powers.note: As described in 1 Kings 4:21-24 and 2 Samuel 8: from the Euphrates (Tiphsah) to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt, with Edom, Moab, Ammon and Aramean states as subject or tributary. Extent debated; no external text confirms it. Tiphsah's location is uncertain.
powers.source: schematic, drawn from the biblical text (1 Kgs 4:21-24; 9:26; 2 Sam 8; 2 Chr 8:4); see sources for the debate

powers.name: Philistia

capital.name: Gath (Tell es-Safi)
capital.coordSource: Approximate site coordinates for Tell es-Safi (not in Pleiades); location described by A. M. Maeir, Bible and Interpretation, 2001.

powers.note: Philistine city-states of the southern coastal plain (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath). Gath (Tell es-Safi) appears to have been the leading city in the 10th–9th centuries BC.
powers.source: schematic, after Maeir (Bible and Interpretation); coast and Shephelah edge

powers.name: Phoenicia
powers.note: Independent city-states (Tyre, Sidon, Byblos, Arwad) on the narrow coastal strip below the Lebanon range. Hiram of Tyre was Solomon's partner (1 Kgs 5).
powers.source: schematic, after the Met essay "The Phoenicians"; coast to Lebanon foothills

powers.name: Aram (Zobah, Damascus)
powers.note: Aramean kingdoms of inland Syria; their 10th-century borders are unknown, so only a label is shown.
powers.source: label only

powers.name: Moab
powers.note: Plateau east of the Dead Sea between the Zered (Wadi al-Hasa) and the Arnon (Wadi Mujib), with the Dibon tableland just north of the Arnon.
powers.source: schematic, after the Mesha Stele (World History Encyclopedia); limits follow the Dead Sea, the Arnon and Zered wadis and the desert edge

powers.name: Ammon
powers.note: Small kingdom around Rabbah on the upper Jabbok (Zarqa); its western limit with Gilead was contested.
powers.source: schematic; limits follow the upper Jabbok and the desert edge

powers.name: Edom

capital.name: Bozrah (Busayra)
capital.coordSource: Approximate: Busayra lies c. 10 km south of Tafila (Encyclopaedia Judaica, "Bozrah"); not in Pleiades.

powers.note: Highlands east of the Arabah, south of the Zered.
powers.source: schematic; limits follow the Zered, the Arabah and the desert edge

powers.name: Egypt
powers.note: Third Intermediate Period Egypt (21st–22nd dynasties). Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) campaigned in Canaan c. 925 BC (1 Kgs 14:25).
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1000.geojson (feature "Egypt"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

periods.debate: The extent of the united monarchy is one of the most disputed questions in biblical archaeology. Israel Finkelstein's "Low Chronology" redates many monumental buildings once attributed to Solomon to the 9th century, leaving a small Jerusalem-based chiefdom; Amihai Mazar keeps a modified traditional chronology and a more substantial early kingdom; Yosef Garfinkel argues from Khirbet Qeiyafa (c. 1020–980 BC) for a fortified Judahite state. The historical-basemaps dataset has a large "Kingdom of David and Solomon" polygon; it was deliberately not used because it presents a maximal reading as an approximate border.

sources.title: Debating the United Monarchy: Let's See How Far We've Come (Zachary Thomas, Biblical Theology Bulletin 46, 2016)
The United Monarchy: Rereading the Bible and the Archaeological Evidence (Lawrence H. Schiffman)
Tell es-Safi/Gath (Aren M. Maeir)

periods.name: Divided kingdom
periods.summary: After Solomon the northern tribes formed the kingdom of Israel (capital Samaria from Omri on), while Judah kept Jerusalem and the line of David. Israel fought and allied with Aram-Damascus, and both faced the advance of Assyria, which received Jehu's tribute and finally destroyed Israel in 722 BC. Moab, Ammon and Edom regained independence; the Mesha Stele records Moab's revolt against Omri's house.

powers.name: Israel
powers.note: Northern kingdom: Galilee, the Jezreel valley, the hill country of Samaria and Gilead east of the Jordan. Gilead and the Ramoth-gilead area were repeatedly lost to Aram; the coastal plain's status varied.
powers.source: schematic, after Bible Odyssey "The Borders of Judah" and Maeir (Bar-Ilan); limits follow the Jordan, the Sea of Galilee, Mt Carmel and the desert edge

powers.name: Judah
powers.note: Southern kingdom: Judean hills, Shephelah and Negev, with its northern border near Bethel and Mizpah.
powers.source: schematic, after Bible Odyssey "The Borders of Judah"; limits follow the Dead Sea, the Negev and the Shephelah edge

powers.name: Aram-Damascus
powers.note: Aramean kingdom of Damascus, strongest under Hazael (late 9th century BC), who took Gilead and destroyed Gath. Its borders are not known well enough to draw.
powers.source: label only

powers.name: Phoenicia
powers.note: Tyre and Sidon and the northern coastal cities. Ethbaal, Jezebel's father, was "king of the Sidonians" (1 Kgs 16:31).
powers.source: schematic, after the Met essay "The Phoenicians"

powers.name: Philistia
powers.note: Philistine cities; Gath led until its destruction (probably by Hazael, late 9th century BC), after which Ashdod and Ekron were the main centres.
powers.source: schematic, after Maeir (Bible and Interpretation)

powers.name: Moab
powers.note: Shown after Mesha's revolt (mid-9th century BC), when Moab recovered the Medeba plain north of the Arnon. Earlier Omri held that area.
powers.source: schematic, after the Mesha Stele (World History Encyclopedia)

powers.name: Ammon
powers.note: Kingdom around Rabbah on the upper Jabbok.
powers.source: schematic

capital.name: Bozrah (Busayra)

powers.note: Edom broke free of Judah in the reign of Jehoram (2 Kgs 8:20-22).
powers.source: schematic

powers.name: Assyria
powers.note: Assyria's core before its great westward expansion. From the 850s BC Shalmaneser III campaigned west (the battle of Qarqar, 853 BC, against a coalition including Ahab); Tiglath-pileser III and Sargon II turned Israel into provinces (732–722 BC).

periods.name: Assyrian Empire
periods.summary: At its height under Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, Assyria ruled from the Zagros to the Mediterranean and, for a time after 671 BC, Egypt. Israel had become Assyrian provinces; Judah survived Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC as a tribute-paying vassal and lost much of the Shephelah. Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC, and Assyrian rule ended by 609 BC.

powers.name: Assyria
powers.note: Zone of provinces and vassal states at its height under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal (c. 680–640 BC); borders were zones of control, not fixed lines. The desert interior was not governed.
powers.source: schematic, after the Met essay "Assyria, 1365–609 B.C." and Maeir (Bar-Ilan); coast from Natural Earth; Urartu (dataset) removed

powers.name: Judah (vassal)
powers.note: Tribute-paying vassal of Assyria after 701 BC, reduced by the loss of much of the Shephelah.
powers.source: schematic, after Maeir (Bar-Ilan) and Bible Odyssey

powers.name: Egypt
powers.note: Ruled by the Kushite 25th dynasty until Assyria took Memphis (671 BC); then Assyrian vassals, and from c. 656 BC the independent 26th (Saite) dynasty.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc700.geojson (feature "Egypt"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Kush
powers.note: Nubian kingdom of Napata whose kings ruled Egypt as the 25th dynasty; Tirhakah (2 Kgs 19:9) was one of them.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc700.geojson (feature "Kush"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Urartu
powers.note: Assyria's northern rival around Lake Van (biblical Ararat, 2 Kgs 19:37).
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc700.geojson (feature "Urartu"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Elam
powers.note: Kingdom of south-west Iran; Ashurbanipal sacked Susa c. 646 BC.

periods.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
periods.summary: Nebuchadnezzar II defeated Egypt at Carchemish (605 BC) and took over the Assyrian lands west of the Euphrates ("Hatti-land"). Jerusalem was captured in 597 BC and destroyed in 587/586 BC, and many of its people were deported to Babylonia. Media ruled the Iranian plateau and eastern Anatolia; Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC.

powers.name: Babylonia
powers.note: Mesopotamia and the Levant under Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BC); borders were zones of control. Nabonidus later lived at Tayma in Arabia for about ten years.
powers.source: schematic, after the Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5) and the Encyclopedia of the Bible; coast from Natural Earth

powers.name: Judah
powers.note: Babylonian vassal from 604 BC; its last kings rebelled. After 586 BC it became a province governed from Mizpah.
powers.source: schematic, after Bible Odyssey

powers.name: Egypt
powers.note: Saite (26th dynasty) Egypt, Babylon's rival for the Levant.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc700.geojson (feature "Egypt"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Media
powers.note: Median kingdom; with Babylon it destroyed Assyria. Its extent is poorly known.
powers.source: label only

powers.name: Lydia
powers.note: Western Anatolian kingdom; its border with Media was fixed at the Halys river (585 BC).
powers.source: label only

powers.name: Tayma
powers.note: Arabian oasis where Nabonidus resided c. 552–543 BC.
powers.source: Pleiades

periods.debate: Where Babylonian authority ended and Median authority began in northern Mesopotamia and the Zagros is uncertain. historical-basemaps has no file between 700 BC and 500 BC, so this empire is drawn schematically.

periods.name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
periods.summary: Cyrus and his successors built the largest empire yet, from the Aegean and Egypt to Central Asia, governed through satrapies. Judah became the small province of Yehud within the satrapy "Beyond the River" (Eber-Nari), with considerable internal autonomy; exiles returned to rebuild the temple. Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Haggai and Zechariah belong to this world.

powers.name: Persian Empire
powers.note: Extent under Darius I (c. 500 BC), including Egypt, Libya and Thrace; satraps could act quite independently, and outer regions were held loosely.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc500.geojson (feature "Achaemenid Empire"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Yehud
powers.note: Small province around Jerusalem, roughly from Bethel/Mizpah to Beth-zur and from the Jordan valley to the hill-country edge. Its exact borders are debated.
powers.source: schematic, after Bible Odyssey "The Borders of Judah" and Finkelstein 2010

powers.name: Samaria (province)
powers.note: Neighbouring province, governed by Sanballat and his family from the late 5th century BC (Neh 4).
powers.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, "Eber-Nari"

powers.name: Susa
powers.note: Royal residence and administrative centre; setting of Esther and Nehemiah 1.
powers.source: Pleiades

periods.debate: The borders of Yehud, and whether they grew between the 6th and 4th centuries BC, are debated (seal-impression studies, the town lists in Nehemiah). Satrapy lists differ between Persian inscriptions and Herodotus, and satrapy borders are not known in detail.

periods.name: Hellenistic kingdoms
periods.summary: After Alexander (died 323 BC) his generals' dynasties divided the East. The Ptolemies of Alexandria held Judea for a century until Antiochus III of the Seleucids defeated them in 200 BC. Seleucid rule led to the crisis under Antiochus IV and the Maccabean revolt (167 BC), the background to Daniel 11 and 1–2 Maccabees. Rome was already advancing into the Greek East.

powers.name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
powers.note: Egypt with Cyrenaica and Cyprus. The dataset still includes southern Syria (Coele-Syria), which Antiochus III took in 200 BC; treat that part as the situation just before.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc200.geojson (feature "Ptolemaic Kingdom"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Seleucid Kingdom
powers.note: From western Anatolia to Iran; capital Antioch on the Orontes.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc200.geojson (feature "Seleucid Kingdom"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Macedon
powers.note: Antigonid Macedon and its Greek allies, soon to be defeated by Rome (197 BC). Only the mainland part of the dataset polygon is kept; its island parts (e.g. Crete) were not Antigonid.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc200.geojson (feature "Macedon and Hellenic League"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Pergamon
powers.note: Attalid kingdom, an ally of Rome.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc200.geojson (feature "Pergamon"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Rome

powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc200.geojson (feature "Rome"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc200.geojson (feature "Parthia"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

periods.name: Roman world in Jesus' time
periods.summary: Rome ruled the Mediterranean; Parthia was its rival in the east. Herod the Great's kingdom had been divided in 4 BC: Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea, Philip the north-eastern districts, and Judea with Samaria and Idumea had become a Roman prefecture in AD 6, governed from Caesarea (Pontius Pilate, AD 26–36). The Gospels move between these jurisdictions.

powers.name: Roman Empire
powers.note: Roman provinces and client kingdoms. The dataset outline is for 1 BC; Cappadocia and Commagene were annexed in AD 17, and the Herodian territories are drawn separately below.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1.geojson (feature "Roman Empire"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Judea (Roman prefecture)
powers.note: Judea, Samaria and Idumea under an equestrian prefect at Caesarea Maritima (from AD 6). Coastal cities such as Gaza were not part of it.
powers.source: schematic, after Josephus, Jewish War 2.96, and the Vanderbilt chapter

powers.name: Antipas: Galilee and Perea
powers.note: Tetrarchy of Herod Antipas (4 BC–AD 39), in two parts: Galilee west of the lake, and Perea east of the Jordan (separated by Decapolis and Samaritan territory). Capital Sepphoris, then Tiberias from c. AD 19.
powers.source: schematic, after Josephus, Jewish War 2.95, and the Vanderbilt chapter; limits follow the Jezreel valley, the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan

powers.name: Philip's tetrarchy
powers.note: Gaulanitis, Batanea, Trachonitis and Auranitis, ruled by Philip (4 BC–AD 34) from Caesarea Philippi.
powers.source: schematic, after Josephus, Jewish War 2.95; limits follow the upper Jordan, the Sea of Galilee, the Yarmuk and the Hauran

powers.name: Decapolis
powers.note: League of Greek cities (Gerasa, Gadara, Scythopolis and others) under the governor of Syria; not a single territory.

powers.name: Syria (province)

powers.source: label only

powers.name: Parthian Empire
powers.note: Rome's great rival in the east; "Parthians, Medes and Elamites" (Acts 2:9) came from its lands.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1.geojson (feature "Parthian Empire"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

periods.name: Roman world in Paul's time
periods.summary: Paul's journeys ran through the Roman provinces of the eastern Mediterranean: Syria and Cilicia, Cyprus, Galatia, Asia, Macedonia and Achaia, and finally by sea past Crete and Malta to Italy. Province names in Acts and the letters (Galatia, Asia, Achaia) refer to these Roman units, which is why the map labels provinces rather than drawing their borders, which are known only approximately.

powers.name: Roman Empire
powers.note: Outline for 1 BC from the dataset, with Judea and Thrace (annexed AD 6 and AD 46) added. Internal province borders are not drawn.

powers.name: Syria and Cilicia
powers.note: Paul's base at Antioch (Gal 1:21). Eastern Cilicia was administered with Syria until Vespasian created a separate province Cilicia (AD 72).

powers.name: Cilicia

powers.name: Cyprus
powers.note: Senatorial province under a proconsul at Paphos (Sergius Paulus, Acts 13:7). The province is the island.
powers.source: Natural Earth 1:50m land (island outline)

powers.name: Galatia
powers.note: Large province including Lycaonia and Pisidia (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe), the churches of Galatians on the "south Galatian" view.
powers.source: label only; capital from Pleiades

powers.name: Asia
powers.note: Proconsular province of western Anatolia; Ephesus was its leading city and the proconsul's usual seat.
powers.source: label only; capital from Pleiades

powers.name: Macedonia
powers.note: Province with Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea (Acts 16–17); governed from Thessalonica.
powers.source: label only; capital from Pleiades

powers.name: Achaia
powers.note: Province of southern Greece governed from Corinth (the proconsul Gallio, Acts 18:12).
powers.source: label only; capital from Pleiades

powers.name: Crete
powers.note: Part of the province Creta et Cyrenaica, governed from Gortyn; the province also included Cyrenaica in Libya (not drawn). Paul's ship sheltered at Fair Havens (Acts 27:8).
powers.source: Natural Earth 1:50m land (island outline)

powers.name: Italia
powers.note: Italy, governed directly from Rome; Paul arrived via Puteoli (Acts 28:13-16).
powers.source: label only; capital from Pleiades

powers.name: Judaea
powers.note: Province under procurators at Caesarea (Felix, Festus, Acts 23–26); parts of Galilee and Perea belonged to Agrippa II.
powers.source: label only; capital from Pleiades

powers.name: Nabataean Kingdom
powers.note: Still a client kingdom (annexed AD 106). Paul went to "Arabia" after his conversion (Gal 1:17).
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1.geojson (feature "Nabatean Kingdom"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

powers.name: Parthian Empire
powers.note: Rome's eastern rival.
powers.source: historical-basemaps world_bc1.geojson (feature "Parthian Empire"), clipped to the Natural Earth coastline and simplified

periods.debate: Whether Paul's "Galatians" lived in the old Celtic north or the southern cities of the province is debated. Provincial boundaries in Anatolia changed several times in the 1st century AD, which is why they are not drawn.
